INTRODUCTION
1. Ms Andrea Kathryn Tracey Schubert (“the practitioner”) has been a registered
psychologist since 1987. She faces two charges of professional misconduct
under s100(1)(a) and s100(1)(b) of the Health Practitioners Competence
Assurance Act 2003 (“the Act”).
2. On 27 June 2014, the Professional Conduct Committee (“PCC”) appointed by
the Psychologists Board of New Zealand, laid charges that between October
2012 and 22 March 2013, the practitioner had been guilty of professional
misconduct because of a failure to maintain appropriate professional
boundaries with two clients that amounted to malpractice or negligence in the
course of the psychologists scope of practice and/or had or was likely to bring
discredit to the profession of psychology.
3. The practitioner denies the charges.
THE CHARGES
4. The charges as laid were amended by consent at the hearing. The charges as
amended are set out below.
Charge 1 – s100(1)(a) – malpractice or negligence
1. That, in terms of section 100(1)(a) of the Act, you have been guilty of
professional misconduct because of one or more acts or omissions that
amount to malpractice or negligence in relation to the ‘psychologist’
scope of practice in that in the course and/or context of the provision by
you of psychological services to your clients, Ms S [“Ms S”] and Mr E
[“Mr E”], in the form of sessions with Ms S and Mr E and of joint
“couples counseling” sessions with both Ms S and Mr E, you acted
inappropriately and/or failed to maintain appropriate professional
boundaries with Ms S and/or Mr E, in one or more of the following ways:
2

a. At times between late October 2012 and 22 March 2013, you created
or entered into separate relationships with each of Ms S and Mr E
which were unnecessarily and/or inappropriately personal and/or
unprofessional and/or which were not consistent with and/or which
had the potential to harm and/or did harm a purpose for which your
services as a psychologist had been engaged, namely to assist both
Ms S and Mr E with relationship issues in that:
i. Between 31 October 2012 and 22 March 2013, you
communicated with Ms S and/or with Mr E inappropriately by
engaging in the email and text message communications that
are set out in the schedule that is provided with this notice;
and/or
ii. On 5 January 2013, you invited Ms S to attend a local jazz
concert with you; and/or
iii. In mid-January 2013, you stayed for several days at a holiday
house owned by Ms S in Collingwood; and/or
iv. In mid to late January 2013, you purchased light shades for Ms
S’s house in Collingwood and gave them to her as a gift;
and/or
v. On 30 January 2013, you visited Mr E at his house, provided
gardening advice and/or services to him, had lunch with him
and then went swimming with him at a local beach; and/or
b. On 22 March 2013, you visited Mr E at his house, talked to him
about the complaint that Ms S had made about you to the
Psychologists Board and drank wine with him; and/or
3

c. You breached your obligation of confidentiality to and/or the privacy
rights of Ms S by disclosing to and/or discussing with Mr E, Ms S’s
personal health information without her permission when you visited
Mr E at his house on 22 March 2013; and/or
d. On 14 February 2013 and 21 February 2013 by text message when
you visited Mr E at his house, you exerted pressure on Mr E to
and/or sought that Mr E persuade Ms S to withdraw her complaint
about you and/or sought that Mr E support you in your response to
the complaint.
Charge 2 – s100(1)(b) – discredit to the profession
2. That, in terms of section 100(1)(b) of the Act, you have been guilty of
professional misconduct because of one or more acts or omissions that
has or have brought or was or were likely to bring discredit to the
profession of psychology. (The particulars of this Charge 2 (a) to (d) are
the same as those set out in Charge 1(a) to (d) and so are not repeated
here).
5. In relation to the particulars set out in Charge 1(a)(i) and Charge 2(a)(i), the
email and text communications were attached to the Charges as a Schedule of
Correspondence between the practitioner, the complainant and Mr E from 31
October 2012 to 22 March 2013. This is an extensive schedule running to
some 38 pages of emails and text messages over the period. It is not produced
in full in this decision though portions of this communication will be referred
to in considering the charges.
THE HEARING
6. The hearing before this Tribunal, proceeded on the basis of an agreed statement
of facts and an agreed bundle of documents. The agreed bundle, included:
(a) Email exchanges between the practitioner and the two clients Ms S and
Mr E between 31 October 2012 and 22 March 2013;
4

(b) The complaint to the New Zealand Psychologists Board from the client
Ms S dated 8 March 2013;
(c) Correspondence between the New Zealand Psychologists Board and the
practitioner relating to the complaint;
(d) Text and phone records for the practitioner and the two clients for the
relevant period;
(e) A transcript produced by Ms S of a conversation overheard by her
between Mr E and the practitioner on 26 March 2013;
(f) The decision of the committee of the New Zealand Psychologists Board
(“the Board”) regarding the complaint against the practitioner dated 4
September 2013 together with various documents and affidavits produced
by the practitioner to the Committee;
(g) Correspondence between the Board and the Health and Disability
Commissioner (HDC) regarding the complaint against the practitioner
7. The PCC called four witnesses:
(a) the complainant Ms S (“Ms S”);
(b) Ms F, a friend of the complainant (“Ms F”);
(c) Professor Frederick Seymour, Clinical Psychologist and the Director of
Clinical Psychology Programme at the School of Psychology at the
University of Auckland. Prof. Seymour was called as an independent
expert to provide evidence as to professional boundaries for registered
psychologists;
(d) Mr E (“Mr E”), the former partner of Ms S and patient of the practitioner.
He was summoned to give evidence by the PCC.
8. The practitioner gave evidence and called two witnesses:
5

(a) Mr L, the practitioner’s [ ] (“Mr L”);
(b) Ms C, a former patient of the practitioner (“Ms C”).
7. The complainant, the practitioner and the witnesses, except Prof. Seymour,
were all granted interim name suppression prior to the commencement of the
hearing and those orders remain in place until further order of the Tribunal.
THE FACTS
9. While the hearing was a defended hearing, the parties did present an agreed
statement of facts for the Tribunal. The agreed facts are set out below:
1. Ms Andrea Kathryn Tracey Schubert is a registered psychologist under
the Health Practitioners Competence Assurance Act 1993 (the HPCAA),
registration number 90-00834. Ms Schubert has been a registered
psychologist since 9 September 1987.
2. Ms Schubert has not practised as a psychologist since the complaint
leading to the current charges but, from October 2012 until January
2013, was in private practice as a psychologist in Nelson. Prior to
moving to Nelson, Ms Schubert had practised as a psychologist for 35
years, primarily in Auckland.
3. Ms Schubert worked as a part-time gardener in a rest home whilst trying
to establish a private practice in Nelson. Ms Schubert is still working as
a gardener.
4. While in practice in Nelson, Ms Schubert was engaged by Ms S (known
as Ms S) and her then partner, Mr E, in late October 2012 to assist in
counseling Ms S and Mr E for some personal relationship issues they
were experiencing. Ms Schubert had been recommended to Ms S by a
mutual colleague, Cher Williscroft.
6

5. In total, Ms S and Mr E attended 4 counselling sessions with Ms
Schubert as a couple. Mr E had 4 counselling sessions with Ms Schubert
on his own, and Ms S had 10 counselling sessions with Ms Schubert on
her own. The first session took place on 29 October 2012, and was a
joint session preceded on that day by individual sessions with both Mr E
and Ms S. The final booked joint sessions on 21 January 2013 was
terminated early by Ms S who did not want to proceed with it.
6. During the course of undertaking counseling with Ms Schubert and after
counseling ended, between late October 2012 and 22 March 2013, both
Ms S and Mr E communicated with Ms Schubert by both text and email
in the manner set out in the Schedule to the Notice of Charges.
7. On 5 January 2013, in the course of a telephone conversation between
Ms S and Ms Schubert, there was discussion about a local jazz concert
being held that day.
8. In early January 2013, Ms Schubert and her then [ ], Mr L, rented a
holiday house owned by Ms S in Collingwood for two days.
9. After staying at Ms S’ holiday house in Collingwood, and upon returning
to Nelson, Ms Schubert attended Ms S’ workplace in Nelson and gifted
her a pair of second-hand lampshades for Ms S’ Collingwood house.
10. On 30 January 2013, Mr E collected Ms Schubert in his car from a car
yard in the middle of Nelson and took her to his recently-purchased
house where Ms Schubert provided gardening advice in return for lunch.
On the way back to deliver Ms Schubert to her car they went swimming
at a local beach, at Ms Schubert’s suggestion.
11. After becoming aware of the swimming, Ms S complained to the New
Zealand Psychologists Board (the Board) about Ms Schubert. Ms S
initially submitted her complaint on 11 February 2013 and then redacted
7

it for the purpose of anonymising Mr E’s name. The complaint was then
resubmitted on 8 March 2013.
12. On 12 February 2013, the Board emailed Ms Schubert to inform her that
it had received a complaint about her from Ms S.
13. On 13 February 2013, Ms Schubert emailed Mr E to inform him that the
initial complaint had been made against her by Ms S.
14. On 22 March 2013, Ms Schubert visited Mr E at his house. During that
visit, Ms Schubert and Mr E discussed the complaint Ms S had made
about Ms Schubert. Mr E offered Ms Schubert a glass of wine, and Ms
Schubert accepted this offer.
15. During Ms Schubert’s visit to Mr E on 22 March 2013, Mr E
inadvertently telephoned Ms S and parts of the conversation between Ms
Schubert and Mr E were overheard by Ms S, and her friend Ms F.
16. On another occasion, Ms Schubert asked Mr E if he had considered the
possibility that Ms S was suffering from [ ]. Ms Schubert had not
previously raised this possibility with Ms S due to no longer being in
contact with Ms S as a result of the complaints process.
17. On 14 February 2013, Ms Schubert sent a text message to Mr E asking
him if he would ask Ms S to withdraw the complaint. On 21 February
2013, in a telephone discussion, Ms Schubert followed up the request to
Mr E by asking him if he’d spoken to Ms S about withdrawing the
complaint.
10. During the course of the hearing, evidence was also given by the witnesses.
The contested evidence is the subject of Tribunal findings as set out in this
decision.
8

THE CODE OF ETHICS FOR PSYCHOLOGISTS
11. The New Zealand Psychologists Board has a code of ethics for all registered
psychologists, setting standards for professional conduct including guidance on
the client-professional boundaries. The “Code of Ethics for Psychologists
working in Aoteroa /New Zealand 2002” (“the Code”) is the relevant code
applicable at the time of the events the subject of these charges.
12. The Code is based around four ethical principles:
(a) Principle 1 - Respect for the dignity of persons and peoples;
(b) Principle 2 - Responsible caring;
(c) Principle 3 - Integrity of relationships;
(d) Principle 4 - Social justice and responsibility to society.
13. There are also value statements and “practice implications” contained in the
Code which outline professional behavior set out in the Code. The practice
implications of most relevance are set out below:
1.6 Principle 1 – Privacy and confidentiality: Psychologists recognise and
promote persons’ and peoples’ rights to privacy. They also recognise
that there is a duty to disclose to appropriate people real threats to the
safety of individuals and the public.
Practice implications
1.6.1 Psychologists make themselves aware of relevant Acts and
Standards and follow procedures that provide for informed
consent, confidentiality, fair treatment and due process as laid
out in those Acts and Standards.
1.6.2 Psychologists explain clearly the measures they will take to
protect confidentiality when engaged in services to, or research
9

with, individuals, families, groups or organisations.
…
1.6.9 Psychologists do not disclose personal information obtained
from an individual, family, whanau or community group or
colleague without the informed consent of those who provided
the information, except in circumstances provided for in 1.6.10.
1.6.10 Psychologists recognise that there are certain exceptions and/or
limitations to non-disclosure of personal information, and
particular circumstances where there is a duty to disclose.
These are:
…
(c) Urgent need: Where a situation arises when it is
impossible or impracticable to seek consent to disclosure
in time to prevent harm or injury to the person, persons,
family whanau, or community group.
…
(e) Client or public safety: Where a psychologist believes that
non-disclosure may endanger a client, research
participant or another person but is denied permission to
disclose, the psychologist exercises professional judgment
in deciding whether to breach confidentiality or not.
Comment
(e) Psychologists should consult with senior colleagues before
making their decision. Ultimately, they must be able to
justify the decision made.
10

Principle 2 – Responsible caring
2.1 Promotion of Well-being: Psychologists’ recognise that a basic ethical
expectation of our discipline is that its activities will benefit members of
society or, at the very least, do no harm.
Practice implications
2.1.1 Psychologists assess the potential harm and benefits involved in
their actions, to predict the likelihood of their occurrence and
proceed only if the potential benefits outweigh the potential
harms. They endeavor to correct any harmful effects that have
occurred because of their activities.
2.1.2 Psychologists use the most respectful and effective interventions
or strategies for those with whom they are working.
…
Principle 3 - Integrity in relationships
…..Expectations of professional practice include: respect, accuracy and
honesty; openness, maintenance of appropriate boundaries, and
avoidance of conflicts of interest. Psychologists will seek to do right in
their relations with others…
3.3 Structure of relationships: Psychologists take responsibility to maintain
appropriate structure in their relationships with persons and peoples
with whom they work.
Practice implications
3.3.1 Psychologists clarify and make explicit their role and
responsibilities with the person(s) with whom they are
working.
11

3.3.2 Psychologists maintain appropriate boundaries with those
with whom they work and carefully consider their actions in
order to maintain their role.
3.4 Conflicts of interest: Psychologists recognise that conflicts of interest
are a threat to the integrity of relationships.
Practice implications
3.4.1 Psychologists seek to avoid dual relationships where that
might present a conflict of interest.
3.4.2 Where dual relationships are unavoidable, psychologists
identify any real or potential conflicts of interest and take all
reasonable steps to address the issue in the best interests of the
parties.
3.4.3 Psychologists do not exploit any work relationship to further
their own personal or business interests.
14. The Code is relevant to determining the standards to be expected of a registered
psychologist and therefore whether any acts or omissions amount to
professional misconduct. However, equally, care must be taken to ensure that
the Code is not automatically used to establish professional misconduct. The
Code is a guide to be taken into account by the Tribunal when it is exercising
its independent judgment as to whether professional misconduct has occurred
in a particular case.1
Expert evidence
15. The Tribunal was also assisted by the independent expert evidence of Professor
Seymour as to the general expectations and practice standards relevant to
1 Collie v Nursing Council of New Zealand [2000] NZAR 74 at [30] and Staite v Psychologists Board
HC Christchurch AP52/98, 18 December 1998
12

professional boundaries for registered psychologists. This evidence included
Professor Seymour’s expert opinion on issues that arise when parallel or dual
personal relationships are formed between psychologist and client.
16. Professor Seymour stated that maintaining professional boundaries is integral
to the ethical and professional practice of psychology. In psychological
practice, and in therapy in particular, a client (or clients where they are in
couple therapy) typically present in a state of psychological illhealth and/or
distress which demands a special duty of care arising from this client
vulnerability. The client must feel safe in the relationship and must believe
their interests will always be paramount in this relationship.
17. Professor Seymour gave a number of reasons why such boundaries are critical:2
(a) If the practitioner blends the professional relationship with another
parallel relationship with a client, either personal or business, then the
client may doubt that their interests will override those of the
psychologist.
(b) The client may also modify their behaviour due to the parallel
relationship (eg: wanting to show themselves in a positive light if a
friendship is developing or already developed) thereby reducing the
benefit of the professional relationship for the client.
(c) There is a power differential in a psychologist – client relationship due to
the personal disclosures made by the client which the psychologist does
not reciprocate. This is appropriate as the needs and goals of the client
are paramount. Therefore the situation is not a naturally occurring
friendship involving the reciprocal exchange of personal information.
This power differential is also likely to remain outside the therapy
relationship.
2 Professor Seymour, statement of evidence, at [16] – [18]
13

(d) Any dual relationship with a client also creates a risk that the practitioner
will reduce their objectivity in their work with that client. The focus of
the relationship may shift to accommodate the practitioner’s own needs
in the dual relationship. This creates the potential for poorer therapeutic
outcomes and/or harm to the client.
18. Professor Seymour also explained that boundary transgressions exist on a
continuum with sexual relations at the most serious, through to relatively minor
transgressions at the other end, (such as borrowing a book from a client).
However, seemingly harmless boundary crossing may lead to a gradual erosion
of the professional relationship as there might be a series of boundary
transgressions which start with minor events but progress or culminate into a
breach of professional boundaries.3
19. The expert evidence was that, in general, pursuing a dual relationship with a
client is inappropriate. This is particularly the case in relation to what are
called “intentional” boundary transgressions, where the psychologist initiates
the social or personal contact. This type of transgression is in the control of the
practitioner and should almost always be avoided as it is highly likely to reduce
the psychologist’s objectivity and disrupt the psychologist-client relationship.4
20. Professor Seymour also noted that general practice standards, including the
Code, recognise that there will be times where a dual relationship is not always
avoidable. These “unintentional” boundary transgressions may arise where the
health practitioner and the client are invited to the same social function or they
unexpectedly meet each other at a community or school event. In this situation,
it remains for the practitioner to exercise their professional judgment as to the
best way to manage the situation in the best interests of the client.
3 Professor Seymour, statement of evidence, at [24] – [25]
4 Professor Seymour, statement of evidence, at [26] – [29]
14

21. Professor Seymour also acknowledged that there is within the profession
recognition that dual relationships are not automatically prohibited or harmful.5
Some authors argue that dual relationships are only harmful if exploitative and
may even hold benefits for a client and the therapeutic process, while
acknowledging the greater complexity that arises from dual relationships.6
However, it was Professor Seymour’s view that where possible boundary
transgressions should be avoided because of the risk that they will disrupt the
psychologist-client relationship.7
22. In his evidence, Professor Seymour commented that in couples’ therapy and
particularly in relation to a couple that was living apart, the psychologist should
have a heightened awareness of the need to strictly observe professional
boundaries. This is because the couples are in a vulnerable and possibly in an
insecure state therefore there is a heightened risk that clients may be looking
for any indicators of bias by the therapist and boundary transgressions therefore
carry greater risks.8
23. The Professor was clear that the Code requires the health practitioner and not
the client to be responsible for ensuring that professional boundaries are
maintained, including where the client initiates contact outside therapy
sessions.
24. The Tribunal was referred to a recognised framework of questions that are a
useful guide for psychologists who face the dilemma as to whether a dual
relationship is appropriate.9
(a) Is the dual relationship necessary?
5 Professor Seymour, statement of evidence at [34] and E Britt & A Kalders, Client – Professional
Relationships (2007) NZ ed., Chapter 11, at [181] – [191]
6 E Britt & A Kalders, at [183]
7 Professor Seymour, statement of evidence at [39]
8 Transcript, Professor Seymour evidence, p217
9 Prof. Seymour, Statement of Evidence, at [36] and his reference to JN Younggren, Ethical decision-
making and dual relationships, (2002), http:/www.kspope.co/dual/younggren.php]:
15

(b) Is the dual relationship exploitative?
(c) Who does the relationship benefit?
(d) Is there a risk that the relationship could damage the client?
(e) Is there a risk that the dual relationship could disrupt the client-
psychologist relationship?
(f) Am I being objective in my evaluation of the matter?
(g) Have I adequately documented the decision making process in my notes?
(h) Did the client give informed consent regarding the risks of engaging in
the dual relationship?
25. Working with a client outside the traditional office environment is a recognised
component of a range of therapies, but it also raises the potential for dual
relationships and therefore needs careful navigation. It is therefore
recommended that the psychologist prepares the client well ahead of the limits
of the professional relationship.10
26. Finally, Professor Seymour noted that gifts from or to clients is an area of
contact which may also test professional boundaries. He noted that gifts from
clients should in general be avoided, though a small gift given at the end of the
professional relationship or at Christmas would be viewed as a relatively minor
boundary transgression and could cause offence if not taken. It is a matter for
the practitioner to assess the situation, including any cultural context, as against
the accepted risks of a boundary transgression. However, Professor Seymour
was clear that gifts from the psychologist to the client would be an intentional
boundary transgression and should be therefore avoided given the risks that are
inherent to clients.11
10 E Britt & A Kalders, at [185]
11 Transcript, Professor Seymour, p215-216
16

THE LAW
27. The practitioner is charged with professional misconduct under s100 of the Act,
which provides as follows:
“100 Grounds on which health practitioner may be disciplined
(1) The Tribunal may make any 1 or more of the orders authorised by
section 101 if, after conducting a hearing on a charge laid under
section 91 against a health practitioner, it makes 1 or more findings
that –
(a) the practitioner has been guilty of professional misconduct
because of any act or omission that, in the judgment of the
Tribunal, amounts to malpractice or negligence in relation to
the scope of practice in respect of which the practitioner was
registered at the time that the conduct occurred; or
(b) the practitioner has been guilty of professional misconduct
because of any act or omission that, in the judgment of the
Tribunal, has brought or was likely to bring discredit to the
profession that the health practitioner practised at the time that
the conduct occurred.”
Professional Misconduct
28. The Tribunal and the Courts have considered the term “professional
misconduct” under s100(1)(a) and (b) of the Act on numerous occasions. The
Tribunal draws on the guidance now available in those cases.12
29. In Collie v Nursing Council, Gendall J states at paragraph [21]:
“Negligence or malpractice may or may not be sufficient to constitute
professional misconduct and the guide must be standards applicable by
12 PCC v Nuttall, (8/Med04/03P), Collie v Nursing Council of New Zealand, [2000] NZAR 74,
17

competent, ethical and responsible practitioners and there must be
behaviour which falls seriously short of that which is to be considered
acceptable and not mere inadvertent error, oversight or for that matter
carelessness.”
30. In Nuttall, the Tribunal has previously adopted the following test of
negligence13;
“The test as to what constitutes negligence in section 100(1)(a) of the
[Act] requires, as a first step in the analysis, a determination of whether
or not, in the Tribunal’s judgment, the practitioners acts or omissions fall
below the standards reasonably expected of a health practitioner in the
circumstances of the person appearing before the Tribunal. Whether or
not there has been a breach of the appropriate standards is measured
against the standards of a responsible body of the practitioner’s peers.”
31. The Tribunal has also consistently adopted common usage definitions of
“malpractice” as being:
“the immoral, illegal or unethical conduct or neglect of professional duty.
Any incidence of improper professional conduct” 14; and
“Improper treatment or culpable negligence of a patient by a physician or
of a client by a lawyer… a criminal or illegal action: common
misconduct.”15
32. Malpractice is a broader notion than negligence. In Re O, the Tribunal said:16
“Malpractice, although often equated with negligence, is perhaps better
considered a broader concept, capable of encompassing neglect, but also
of extending to trespassory conduct in the process of caring for patients in
Aladdin 12/Den05/04D and 13/Den04/02D and Dale 20/Nur05/09D
13 PCC v Nuttall, supra at [62]
14 Collins English Dictionary, 2nd Edition
15 The New Shorter Oxford Dictionary, 1993 Edition.
16 Re Mrs O 104/Psy07/58D (HPDT) citing Manning, Dawson, Peart, Brookbanks, Medical Law in
18

relation to consent, breaches of patient confidence and fiduciary
obligations, and other forms of conduct reaching the necessary level of
gravity, such as assaulting a patient, swearing at or threatening a patient,
a deliberate failure to obey an instruction or sexual misconduct.”
33. The concepts of negligence and malpractice are both possible forms of
professional misconduct, they are similar and are not mutually exclusive. In
PCC v Nuttall, the Tribunal recognised that it is “quite conceivable for acts or
omissions to constitute both malpractice and negligence”17
34. It is for the Tribunal to determine whether the conduct has or is likely to bring
discredit on the psychology profession under s.100(1)(b) of the Act. In Collie
at [28], Gendall J discussed the meaning of this provision, under the previous
legislation, and stated:
“To discredit is to bring harm to the repute or reputation of the
profession. The standard must be an objective standard for the question to
be asked by the Council being whether reasonable members of the public,
informed and with the knowledge of all the factual circumstances, could
reasonably conclude that the reputation and good-standing of the nursing
profession was lowered by the behaviour of the nurse concerned.”
35. There is a well-established two stage test for determining professional
misconduct set out in previous decisions of both this Tribunal and its
predecessor.18 The two key steps involved in assessing what constitutes
professional misconduct are:
(a) First, an objective analysis of whether the practitioner’s acts or omissions
can reasonably be regarded by the Tribunal as constituting malpractice,
negligence or otherwise bringing or likely to bring discredit on the
profession; and
New Zealand (2006, Brookers, Wellington)
17 PCC v Nuttall 8/Med04/03P (HPDT) at [59]
18 McKenzie v MPDT [2004] NZAR 47 at [71] and PCC v Nuttall (8/Med04/03P)
19

(b) Secondly, the Tribunal must be satisfied that the practitioner’s acts or
omissions require a disciplinary sanction for the purposes of protection of
the public or maintaining professional standards or punishing the
practitioner.
36. The Tribunal is mindful that the burden of proof in the present case is on the
PCC. This means that it is for the PCC to establish that the practitioner is
guilty of professional misconduct. The PCC must produce the evidence that
establishes the charge to the appropriate standard of proof.
37. The standard of proof is the civil standard of proof, that is proof which satisfies
the Tribunal that on the balance of probabilities the particulars of the charge are
more likely than not. The Tribunal must apply a degree of flexibility to the
balance of probabilities taking into account the seriousness of the allegation,
and the gravity of the consequences flowing from a particular finding.19
38. The Tribunal is also required to consider each particular independently and
then cumulatively, in the context of determining whether the overall charge is
established.20
Jurisdiction issue
39. At the outset of the hearing, counsel for the practitioner raised a preliminary
question as to the jurisdiction of the Tribunal in respect of the charges. The
Tribunal notes at the outset we do not consider this is properly an issue as to
“jurisdiction” in the sense of the functions, powers and duties of the Tribunal.
It is a submission as to the nature of the charge.
40. It is submitted for the practitioner that the wording of charge 1(a) is such that it
restricts the Tribunal to only being able to consider those acts or omissions
alleged against the practitioner which took place inside the counselling sessions
19 Z v Complaints Assessment Committee [2009] 1 NZLR 1 and followed by this Tribunal in PCC v
Karagiannis 181/Phar08/91P
20 Duncan v Medical Practitioners Disciplinary Committee [1986] 1 NZLR 513
20

provided to Ms S and Mr E. The practitioner relies upon the wording of the
charge - “the form of sessions with each of [the clients] and of joint “couples
counselling” sessions with both [clients], you acted inappropriately and/or
failed to maintain appropriate professional boundaries.”
41. The PCC maintain that the charge does not require such a restrictive
interpretation, as the professional misconduct alleged is in relation to the
psychologists scope of practice in that “in the course and/or context of the
provision by the practitioner of psychological services to the clients” means
that the sub-particulars of the charge can properly be considered in the course
and/or context of the provision of services.
42. The Tribunal accepts the PCC submission on this matter. The charge is
worded to encompass the acts or omissions by the practitioner in the “course
and/or context” of the provisions of psychological services which are then
described as individual and joint sessions. This does not restrict the Tribunal to
what occurred inside the counselling sessions but imports a wider consideration

asked to take responsibility for her part in the matter.”37
(g) The practitioner discussed the last joint counselling session and her view
as to why Ms S exited the joint session that day. She expressed her
sadness at this to Mr E as she had thought that when the counselling
relationship finished they could have been friends.

(h) She then shared a dream with Mr E in which she had gone to the movies
with Mr E and Ms S had thrown a glass of wine at her. She then joked
about how Ms S would have reacted if they had really gone to the movies
given the reaction of the gardening advice.
(i) The practitioner also responded to Mr E when he asked about a future

(j) They discussed together the possibility that Ms S was having an affair

(k) They also talked about Ms S’s friends and who might be able to support

117. The Tribunal notes that Ms S and Ms F say they heard the last part of the
conversation as being for the purpose of getting friends to persuade Ms S to
give up the complaint. While the Tribunal has no reason to doubt Ms S and Ms
F in their recollection of the call, it is not critical to reconcile these differences
given our findings about the extent of the conversation admitted by the
practitioner.
118. It was not, on any view of it, an appropriate meeting or conversation between
the practitioner and Mr E, when she had only recently been acting as registered
psychologist to both Mr E and Ms S. This was particularly so when there was a
current complaint about a breach of professional boundaries with Mr E. The
meeting and conversation display a significant lack of insight into the
practitioner’s obligations to respect the professional boundary required to
operate about discussing her personal situation with an immediate past client
particularly when it involved that client and another.
119. The practitioner clearly sought the meeting to further her own interests in being
able to discuss the complaint with Mr E and seek more information about Ms
40

S. The practitioner had a conflict of interest operating in this meeting on 22
March 2013. She on the one hand was expressing her concern for Ms S and
her health but at the same time she was attempting to influence Ms S’s decision
to complain and making observations about her possibly unstable mental health
to Mr E. Viewed by any reasonable and competent registered psychologist this
was not in Ms S’s or Mr E’s best interests.
120. The practitioner was also giving Mr E details of her personal position and
sharing her distress about the complaint. This likely had the impact that it
imposed a sense of responsibility on Mr E. In this meeting, Mr E offered to
provide the practitioner with accommodation in his home when she referred to
her financial hardship caused by the complaint.
121. Finally, the meeting with Mr E always carried with it a risk that it would be
discovered by Ms S and cause further distress for her. Unfortunately, the
discovery was more immediate and distressing than could have been
anticipated when Ms S overheard much of the conversation via her mobile
phone that evening.
122. The Tribunal finds this particular of charge 1 established.
Particular 1(c) – The Practitioner breached her obligation of confidentiality
to and/or the privacy of Ms S by disclosing to and/or discussing with Mr E,
her personal health information without her permission when the
Practitioner visited Mr E at his house on 22 March 2013.
123. The Tribunal is satisfied that during the course of the meeting with Mr E on 22
March 2013, the practitioner did discuss Ms S’s personal health information
without her permission.
124. The personal health information included:
(a) her mental health including the possibility that she may have [ ] and the
possibility of [ ] Ms S; and
41

(b) Ms S’s behaviour at the last joint counselling session and the
practitioners evaluation of why Ms S had departed that day; and
(c) Ms S’s family and her family relationships.
125. The practitioner maintained that she only had these discussions out of concern
for Ms S’s well-being and risk to her safety. However, the Tribunal does not
accept this explanation is sufficient to justify the breach of confidentiality and
privacy. There was no evidence of any immediate or urgent threat to Ms S’s
health that required this discussion. If the practitioner was concerned about the
health of the patient then the appropriate action was to raise this concern with
another health professional such as Ms S’s General Practitioner and/or to
discuss the appropriate course of action with the practitioner’s own supervisor.
126. The practitioner also maintained that the disclosure of Ms S’s personal health
information was not a breach of any professional obligation as Ms S had
consented to a full exchange of all personal information with Mr E at the outset
of the joint counselling sessions.
127. However, the personal health information had been obtained for the purpose of
providing psychological services to Ms S. During the course of the meeting
with Mr E, the practitioner was misusing the personal health information, in a
way that appeared to be principally serving her own purposes in discussing her
anxiety over the complaint.38 By 22 March 2014, it was clear that Ms S had
terminated the professional relationship with the practitioner. Therefore, the
practitioner no longer had any consent to discuss Ms S’s personal health
information with Mr E.

128. This particular of charge 1 is established as professional misconduct.

the practitioner exerted pressure on Mr E to and/or sought that Mr E
persuade Ms S to withdraw her complaint about the practitioner and/or
sought that Mr E support the practitioner in her response to the complaint.
129. The practitioner acknowledged that she had sent text messages to Mr E on both
14 and 21 February 2013.
130. These text messages were sent to Mr E after Ms S had lodged her complaint
against the practitioner with the Psychologists Board. On 13 February, the
practitioner had emailed Mr E a copy of the complaint and said “I will need
your support on this as she could well derail me. I feel sick about this. Can we
meet up sometime please”
131. The content of the subsequent text messages is set out below:
14/02/2013 – Practitioner: “Please can u ask [Ms S]2 withdraw her
complaint? If I have to defend myself she is only going 2 b further hurt as she
Will not like what I will say. It will only make matters worse. I am loathe to
do this but she leaves me no choice if she doesnt withdraw it. Somehow I don’t
think she Will but it’s worth u asking. Thanks”
21/02/2013 – Practitioner: “Thanks [Mr E]. No word from t Board, I think they
r waiting 4 [Ms S’s] response 2 withdraw it in full & final. Then they may or
may not take it further, I wud be grateful if u cuddled send me yr draft response

21/02/2013 – Practitioner: “Have u asked [Ms S] if she’s withdrawn t
complaint?”
43

132. Mr E gave evidence that he did not feel pressured by the practitioner’s request.
However, it is evident from the email and text messages set out above that the
practitioner did ask Mr E to get Ms S to withdraw her complaint and sought his
support to defend the complaint.
133. The Tribunal considers that it is wholly inappropriate for a registered
psychologist to enlist and involve a client, or former client, in this way for the
practitioner’s own purposes. The request carried with it the real risk that a
person in Mr E’s position would feel pressured to make the request. This is
particularly so when it was being made clear to Mr E that otherwise there were
likely adverse consequences for his former partner Ms S.
134. The way the request was framed meant it was also likely that Mr E would tell
Ms S that her complaint should be withdrawn to avoid hurt to her (the reason
given by the practitioner). This was likely to cause further distress and anxiety
for Ms S about her decision to complain.
135. Finally, the request also carried the risk that it would put Mr E and Ms S into
further conflict in their relationship as it did.
136. Although, the practitioner stated she was doing it out of concern for Ms S, it
was not a responsible act by a registered health practitioner given the risks the
request carried. The Tribunal finds this particular is established.
Summary of findings in relation to Charge 1
137. The Tribunal findings in relation to the particulars of Charge 1 are summarised
below:
Charge 1(a)(i) – established as professional misconduct both separately and
cumulatively;
Charge 1(a)(ii)-(iv) – established as professional misconduct on a cumulative
basis together with other particulars made out in Charge 1;
44

Charge 1(a)(v) – established as professional misconduct both separately and
cumulatively;
Charge 1(b)-(d) – established as professional misconduct both separately and
cumulatively.
138. We have also considered whether the conduct established amounts to
malpractice or negligence in relation to the psychologist’s scope of practice.
We are satisfied that the nature of the particulars established are a neglect of
professional duty and amount to improper professional conduct of such gravity
that cumulatively they do amount to malpractice.
139. The Tribunal has found that the particulars of Charge 1(a)(ii) to (iv) were not
so serious as to stand as separate acts of malpractice but taken together with the
other more serious breaches of professional obligations, they cumulatively add
to the overall finding of malpractice. The Tribunal also wish to note that the
most serious of the breaches is Charge (1)(a)(v) in relation to the lunch and
swim with Mr E. This was a breach of professional boundaries that was a
significant neglect of professional duties and fell well below the standards
expected of competent registered psychologists.
Charge (2) – s100(1)(b) - Discredit to the Profession
140. This charge is based on the same particulars as Charge 1.
141. The Tribunal is equally satisfied that the particulars as established in relation to
Charge 1 also bring, or are likely to bring, discredit to the psychology
profession and therefore constitute professional misconduct.
142. The breach of professional boundaries by the practitioner with two clients in
such an extensive way and over a period of several months can only bring
discredit to the practitioner’s profession. The conduct established in this case
is not what a reasonable and informed member of the public would expect from
a registered psychologist who is entrusted to provide professional services to a
couple who are at a difficult point in their relationship. The public must have
45

confidence that they can come to a registered psychologist and trust that the
practitioner will not intrude into their personal lives and relationships in the
way this practitioner did.
IS A DISCIPLINARY SANCTION REQUIRED?
143. The Tribunal is satisfied that the conduct established in both charges 1 and 2,
do require a disciplinary sanction. The sanction is required in order to meet the
primary objectives of the Act; namely to protect the public and maintain
appropriate professional standards for the psychology profession. The
practitioner’s conduct as established was a significant departure from
acceptable professional standards for any registered psychologist.
144. It is an essential feature of the trust that is placed in psychologists that they
carry out their duties in a way that does not breach the ethical and professional
boundaries set for the profession.
145. The breach of professional boundaries committed were not minor or
inconsequential. They occurred as a result of the practitioner’s intentional
actions on multiple occasions and over a period of five months. The breaches
of professional boundaries also caused harm; this was evident from Ms S’s
evidence about the distress caused to her as a result of the practitioner’s
decision to have lunch and a swim with Mr E in late January 2013 and the
practitioner’s subsequent behavior towards her. It was clear to the Tribunal
that the relationship between Ms S and Mr E was harmed by the breach of
professional boundaries by the practitioner. The conflict it caused between Ms
S and Mr E meant their relationship was further strained and continued to be so
at the hearing. These are serious matters that require an appropriate
disciplinary sanction.

The professional misconduct charges upheld
9. In summary, the Tribunal found that the charges of professional misconduct had been

follows:
Professional Misconduct
10. Charge 1 –The practitioner was found guilty by this Tribunal of both negligence and
malpractice while operating in her scope or practice. In the course of, and in the
context of, providing psychological services and couples counselling to two clients in
a difficult stage of their relationship, the practitioner failed to maintain appropriate
professional boundaries with both clients. The particulars established were:
(a) Over a five month period, a large volume of email and text communication
sent and received displayed an unnecessary personal communication between
4

the practitioner and her two clients at a time when both clients were in
treatment or had only just finished being in treatment with the practitioner.
(b) An invitation extended by the practitioner to the female client to attend a
local concert together with other friends of the practitioner;
(c) Arrangements made to pay for the hire of, and stay at, the holiday home of the
female client and a gift given by the practitioner to the female client as a
personal thank you for the use of the holiday home;
(d) Accepting an invitation for lunch at the home of the male client and
swimming with him at a local beach with him that same day.
(e) Following a complaint made to the Psychologists Board by the female client
about a swim and lunch between the practitioner and male client, the
practitioner sent two text messages to the male client in which she sought to
have him persuade the female client to withdraw her complaint;
(f) In a later visit to the male client’s home, the practitioner also spoke to him
about the complaint and drank wine with him. During the course of the
conversation the practitioner discussed the female client’s personal health
information without her consent;
11. The Tribunal has previously described the invitation to a concert and the events
surrounding the use of the holiday home as comparatively less serious incidents of
failure to maintain professional boundaries. However, the other breaches are viewed
as more serious breaches of professional boundaries which amount to both
negligence and malpractice.
12. The conduct established above also formed the basis of the Tribunal’s finding that
the practitioners conduct had brought or was likely to bring discredit to the
profession of psychologists under s100(1)(b) of the Act.
Penalty
13. The Tribunal must now go on to consider what penalty may be appropriate under
s101 of the Act. The penalties provided for under s101 include:
5

(a) Cancellation of the health practitioner’s registration;
(b) Suspension of the registration for a period not exceeding 3 years;
(c) An order that the practitioner may only practise his profession in accordance
with conditions imposed as to employment, supervision or otherwise;
(d) Censure;
(e) A fine of up to $30,000; and
(f) An order as to costs of the Tribunal and/or the PCC to be met in part or in
whole by the practitioner.
14. The Tribunal also notes the High Court summation of the appropriate sentencing
principles as set out in Roberts v Professional Conduct Committee.2 Collins J
identified the following eight factors as relevant whenever the Tribunal is
determining an appropriate penalty. In particular, the Tribunal is bound to consider
what penalty:
(a) most appropriately protects the public and deters others;
(b) facilitates the Tribunal’s important role in setting professional standards;
(c) punishes the practitioner;
(d) allows for the rehabilitation of the health practitioner;
(e) promotes consistency with penalties in similar cases;
(f) reflects the seriousness of the misconduct;
(g) is the least restrictive penalty appropriate in the circumstances; and
(h) looked at overall, is the penalty which is “fair, reasonable and proportionate
in the circumstances.”
15. In the subsequent decision of the High Court in Katamat, Williams J adopted the
eight sentencing principles set out in the Roberts decision and went on to summarise
the case law in this way:
2 [2012] NZHC 3354 at [44]-[51], also followed in Katamat v Professional Conduct Committee [2012]
NZHC 1633, 21 December 2012, Williams J.
6

“[53] In summary, the case law reveals that several factors will be relevant to
assessing what penalty is appropriate in the circumstances. Some factors, such as
the need to protect the public and to maintain professional standards, are more
intuitive in their application. Others, such as the seriousness of offending and
consistency with past cases, are more concrete and capable of precise evaluation.
Of all the factors discussed, the primary factor will be what penalty is required to
protect the public and deter similar conduct. The need to punish the practitioner can
be considered, but is of secondary importance. The objective seriousness of the
misconduct, the need for consistency with past cases, the likelihood of rehabilitation
and the need to impose the least restrictive penalty that is appropriate will all be
relevant to the inquiry. It bears repeating, however, that the overall decision is
ultimately one involving an exercise of discretion.”
16. The Tribunal adopts the guidance of the Courts in considering the appropriate
penalty in this case.

penalty for Ms Schubert.
Tribunal’s consideration
37. The aggravating and mitigating features of this case have been considered by the
Tribunal and we have set these out below.
Aggravating features
38. The aggravating features of this case are, in our view:
(a) This misconduct took place in the context of a client couples counselling.
This is a particularly vulnerable setting for clients of health practitioners and
one in which a practitioner must therefore remain vigilant as to any risk of
professional boundary transgression.
(b) The misconduct was not just a one off incident of professional misjudgment.
The charges relate to a period of almost five months over which time the
practitioner committed numerous acts of professional misconduct as detailed
in the charges.
(c) The practitioner also failed to identify for herself what should have been for
an experienced practitioner clear breaches of professional boundaries. This
failure largely continued throughout the PCC investigation of the complaint
and through the Tribunal hearing. It is therefore doubtful that the practitioner
has as yet gained much insight into her offending.
(d) The fact that the practitioner went on, after the initial complaint by Ms S, to
commit further acts of misconduct in meeting with Mr E to discuss the
complaint and disclose confidential information about Ms S was certainly an
aggravating circumstance of the offending.
11

(e) Finally, there was a significant impact for the complainant, Ms S. She gave
detailed evidence at the hearing and in her most recent affidavit of the adverse
impact she has suffered as a result of the practitioner’s breaches of
boundaries. We accept that the complainant has likely suffered considerable
adverse impact and that this remains on-going for her.
Mitigating features
39. The Tribunal is also satisfied that there are some mitigating features in the
practitioner’s favour, including:
(a) Ms Schubert has practised in psychology for 35 years and this is her
first time before this Tribunal;
(b) Ms Schubert does appear to have had a degree of vulnerability at the
time the misconduct occurred. She had only recently moved to Nelson
and was working to establish herself in practice. Ms S and Mr E were
her first clients in Nelson. On her own evidence she did not have many
friends in Nelson and there was no evidence of family support in
Nelson;
(c) There is now some acknowledgement, in hindsight, of the misconduct
as evident by the consent memorandum as to penalty which
acknowledges that a period of suspension and conditions imposed on
her practice are justified.
Decision on penalty
40. The practitioner must clearly understand from this decision that in the main the
findings made against her by this Tribunal are serious and bring the psychology
profession into disrepute. In future, she must conduct herself in accordance with the
professional standards required of a competent, ethical and responsible health
practitioner and she must in future observe strict professional boundaries with
clients.
41. The Tribunal does however acknowledge that the practitioner’s offending is not at
the highest end of offending seen before this Tribunal. The Tribunal is also mindful
12

that this is the practitioner’s first professional misconduct charges in 35 years of
practice.
42. The Tribunal agrees with counsel that suspension in this case is the appropriate and
proportionate penalty rather than cancellation. It is our view that an 18 month period
of suspension is appropriate in the interests of public safety, the maintenance of
professional standards and to serve as a period of reflection and rehabilitation for the
practitioner.
43. It remains important to send a message by this decision to the profession and the
public, that there are serious professional consequences for failure to maintain
appropriate boundaries with clients. It is a fundamental breach of the core ethical
principles for a registered psychologist to enter into social and personal relationships
with clients as the practitioner has in this case.
44. We remain concerned that the practitioner lacks remorse and genuine insight into her
offending. The penalty phase of this proceeding did provide an opportunity for the
practitioner to demonstrate to the Tribunal evidence of any remorse and insight. We
have not had any material evidence of this presented to us. While the practitioner
did, during the course of her evidence, acknowledge some transgressions and
misjudgment, particularly in relation to swimming with Mr E, it did not appear to the
Tribunal that she was remorseful for the damage her actions had caused to the
complainant. The practitioner has not expressed any real remorse or apology for her
offending even at this penalty phase of the proceeding.
45. The Tribunal is also concerned at the subsequent email contact Ms Schubert made
with the complainant after this Tribunal’s decision was delivered on 24 December
2014. This was an extremely inappropriate message for any registered health
professional to send to a former client and particularly so in the circumstances of the
decision just delivered against the practitioner. This appears to show an on-going
lack of insight and remorse by the practitioner.
46. We remain concerned that the practitioner is at some risk that she will re-offend if
she does not accept the need for maintaining appropriate professional boundaries
with clients. We therefore consider it necessary to impose a number of conditions on
the practitioner’s return to practice. In doing so we have taken into account the four
13

conditions as set out in the consent memorandum on penalty as filed by the parties.
The Tribunal has adapted those conditions and also added three further conditions
which we consider are necessary to ensure public safety and to provide the
appropriate opportunity for rehabilitation.
47. The conditions on Ms Schubert’s return to practice, to apply for a further 18 months
from the date of her return to practice, are:
i. The practitioner must only practise as an employee within a private practice,
public agency or other employment setting, in which she receives employer
supervision of her practice. Such employment to be approved by the New
Zealand Psychologists Board;
ii. The practitioner must not work with clients with any mental health conditions
for which diagnoses may be required;
iii. The practitioner must ensure that her practice is performed at the work place
of her employer and not at her home or the home of any client;
iv. The practitioner must undergo a regular and structured supervision
programme with a senior and experienced supervisor as approved by the
Psychologists Board. This supervision is to be provided by a supervisor
working in the city or town in which the practitioner is practising. The
supervisor will report regularly to the Board on the practitioner’s progress
including whether she understands and is willing to maintain appropriate
professional boundaries with clients. The practitioner will meet the costs of
such supervision.
v. The practitioner must satisfy the Psychologists Board that she has undertaken
an appropriate course in Ethics and Professional Boundaries as at the date she
applies to re-commence practice;
vi. The practitioner must satisfy the Psychologists Board that she can provide to
it a current independent psychological assessment which establishes that she
is fit to return to practice as at the date she applies to re-commence practice;
and;
14

vii. The practitioner must not have any further contact with the complainant,
unless the complainant has provided prior consent.
48. There will also be an order for censure of the practitioner. No fine was sought by the
PCC nor does it appear appropriate given Ms Schubert’s apparent lack of means and
legal aid grant.
Name suppression matters
49. Ms Schubert currently has interim name suppression. The Consent Memorandum
signed by counsel confirms that the interim name suppression for the practitioner
should be lifted. It was therefore somewhat surprising to find that the subsequent
submissions on penalty filed for the practitioner now seek name suppression for Ms
Schubert. Nevertheless, we deal with this matter in its merits.
50. In summary, the grounds advanced on behalf of Ms Schubert are that:
(a) Publication of her name will create an undue risk that the complainant Ms S
and the witness Mr E will be identified if the practitioner’s name is not
suppressed. In particular, the matters relied upon are;
i. That Ms S and Mr E have disclosed the fact of the complaint to others;
ii. The community of Nelson is a small community and publication of the
practitioner’s name will lead to identification of the complainant and
Mr E;
(b) The practitioner has had a fragile mental state and there is some risk that
publication of her name could exacerbate her condition.
51. The PCC opposes any permanent name suppression for the practitioner. The PCC
maintains that, as there have now been adverse disciplinary findings made against the
practitioner, the public interest in openness and transparency of such disciplinary
proceedings overrides any private interest of the practitioner.
52. The Tribunal has considered the application in accordance with the requirements of
s95 of the Act. The Tribunal must consider whether it is “desirable” to prohibit
15

publication of the name of the applicant after considering the interest of any person
and the public interest.
53. The Tribunal in Karagiannis,5 has previously confirmed the public interest factors to
include:
(a) Openness and transparency in disciplinary proceedings;
(b) Accountability of the disciplinary process;
(c) Public interest in knowing the identity of the practitioner;
(d) The importance of freedom of speech and the right enshrined in s14, New
Zealand Bill of Rights Act 1990;
(e) Unfairly impugning other practitioners;
(f) Where an adverse disciplinary finding has been made, it is necessary for more
weighty private interest factors to be advanced to overcome the public interest
factors for publication.
54. A useful summary of the private and public interest considerations is also provided
by the High Court in Anderson,6 in which Gendall J states:
“[36] Private interests will include the health interests of a practitioner, matters
that may affect a family and their wellbeing, and rehabilitation. Correspondingly,
interest such as protection of the public, maintenance of professional standards,
both openness and ‘transparency’ and accountability of the disciplinary process,
the basic value of freedom to receive and impart information, the public interest
knowing the identity of a practitioner found guilty of professional misconduct, the
risk of other doctors’ reputations being affected by suspicion, are all factors to be
weighed on the scales.
[37] Those factors were also referred to at some length in the Tribunal. Of course
publication of a practitioner’s name is often seen by the practitioner to be punitive
but its purpose is to protect and advance the public interest by ensuring that it is
informed of the disciplinary process and of practitioners who may be guilty of
5 Karagiannis 181/Phar08/91P
6 Anderson v PCC, CIV 2008-485-1646, 14 November 2008, High Court, Wellington
16

malpractice or professional misconduct. It reflects also the principles of openness
of such proceedings, and freedom to receive and impart information.”
55. The Tribunal is satisfied that the public interest factors in support of the
practitioner’s name being published outweigh the private interest factors relied upon
by Ms Schubert. The openness, transparency and accountability of the Tribunal
process and the public interest in knowing and reporting the identity of the
practitioner is paramount in this case.
56. While we have noted the submissions of the practitioner’s counsel, we do not find
them sufficiently compelling to override the now substantial public interest in
knowing the identity of a practitioner guilty of professional misconduct.
57. The Tribunal is satisfied that by suppressing the names of the complainant and other
factual witnesses and any identifying features of the case including the name of the
city in which the practitioner is living, we can sufficiently protect the identity of Ms
S and Mr E. If they have disclosed their involvement in the case to friends or family
that is a matter for them. It does not justify name suppression for the practitioner in
this case.
58. We have also considered the submission that the practitioner’s mental health may be
put at risk by publication of her name. It is almost inevitably the case that
publication of the practitioners name will have an adverse impact for her. We do not
dismiss this lightly given the practitioner’s evidence at hearing about her admission
to hospital in early 2014 when she was advised of the PCC charges. However, we
have not been presented with any current independent medical or psychological
report that would be required to satisfy the Tribunal that there is a current and
material risk to the practitioner’s health and safety. In the circumstances, there is not
sufficient evidence of any private interest factor that outweighs the public interest
factors in this case.
59. The Tribunal is willing to order permanent name suppression to the complainant, Ms
S and to Mr E and the other witnesses of fact, as outlined in the orders below. It is
desirable to grant name suppression to these parties as there is no public interest in
knowing their names and it is desirable that witnesses are encouraged to give
evidence to the Tribunal without fear of unnecessary publication of their names.
17

Costs
60. In relation to costs, the Tribunal records that it has used as a starting point that a
health practitioner will generally be expected to contribute 50% of the actual and
reasonable costs of the Tribunal and PCC.
61. The costs incurred by the PCC and Tribunal as at 20 March 2015, are $120,866.
These costs do not include the additional costs relating to the penalty hearing which
have not been sought by the PCC.
62. The Tribunal has determined that Ms Schubert is entitled to a modest discount
appropriate to reflect the fact that she did make some effort to reduce costs in relation
to the hearing by agreeing a statement of facts. However, overall Ms Schubert
elected to defend all the charges in a fulsome way over the course of three days of
hearing, as she is entitled to do.
63. We did not have any detailed evidence or any affidavit from the practitioner as to her
financial means that would allow us to make any further discount for financial
circumstances. We did hear some oral evidence from Ms Schubert about her
difficulty in earning an income since these charges were laid and in meeting her
mortgage payments. However, we also had oral evidence from Mr L that Ms
Schubert and he [ ] at the time of hearing. While we acknowledge Ms Schubert is in
receipt of legal aid this does not in itself justify a discount on costs when considering
the order of costs under s45(5) of the Legal Services Act 2011.
64. The Tribunal considers that a reasonable contribution to costs of the PCC and
Tribunal would have been 45% of the total costs and expenses incurred by the PCC
and the Tribunal, but for the grant of legal aid and we make this indication for the
purposes of s45(5) of the Legal Services Act 2011.
Orders of the Tribunal
65. The Tribunal makes the following orders:
(a) The practitioner is suspended from practice for the period of 18 months from
the date of this order.
(b) The practitioner is censured pursuant to section 101(1)(d) of the Act. This
18

censure is to mark the Tribunal’s disapproval of the practitioner’s
professional misconduct;
(c) That in accordance with s100(1)(c) of the Act, the practitioner may, after
commencing practice following the end of the suspension, for a further period
of 18 months, practise her profession only in accordance with the following
conditions:
i. The practitioner must only practise as an employee within a private
practice, public agency or other employment setting in which she
receives employer supervision of her practice, such employment to be
approved by the Psychologist Board;
ii. The practitioner must not work with clients with any mental health
conditions for which diagnoses may be required;
iii. The practitioner must ensure that her practice is performed at the work
place of her employer and not at her home or the home of any client;
iv. The practitioner must undergo a regular and structured supervision
programme with a senior and experienced supervisor as approved by
the Psychologists Board. This supervision is to be provided by a
supervisor working in the city or town in which the practitioner is
practising. The supervisor will report regularly to the Board on the
practitioner’s progress including whether she understands and is willing
to maintain appropriate professional boundaries with clients. The
practitioner will meet the costs of such supervision.
v. The practitioner must satisfy the Psychologists Board that she has
undertaken an appropriate course in Ethics and Professional Boundaries
as at the date she applies to re-commence practice;
vi. The practitioner must provide to the Psychologists Board a current
independent psychological assessment which establishes that she is fit
to return to practise as at the date she applies to re-commence practice;
and
19

vii. The practitioner must not have any further contact with the
complainant, unless the complainant has provided prior consent.
(d) An order as to costs to be met by the practitioner would have been for 45% of
the total costs of the PCC and the Tribunal, were it not for the fact that the
practitioner is in receipt of legal aid. This indication of costs is therefore
made for the purposes of s45(5) of the Legal Services Act 2011.
(e) The Tribunal orders publication of the practitioner’s name. The order for
interim name suppression is discharged and the application for permanent
name suppression is declined.
(f) Permanent name suppression orders are made in relation to Ms S, Ms F, Mr
L, Ms C and Mr E, including a prohibition on publication of any particulars
which may identify them.
(g) The Tribunal directs the Executive Officer to publish a copy of this decision
and a summary of it on the Tribunal website. The Tribunal further directs the
Executive Officer to publish details of this decision on the website of the
New Zealand Psychologists Board and in its magazine.
66. The Tribunal also recommends that the practitioner, prior to resuming practice,
undergoes a period of at least six months counselling to assist her to gain insight into
the breaches of professional boundaries she has committed. This recommendation is
made to assist her rehabilitation and it is hoped that she will take the opportunity to
do so during the period of suspension.
